title: NGS Data Structures in R
text:
Introduction
These notes accompany the NGS Data Analysis module.
They focus on the SummarizedExperiment family of R/Bioconductor objects — the standard container for virtually every modern high-throughput sequencing analysis pipeline.

title: NGS Data Structures in R
text:
Why a dedicated container?
NGS experiments produce at least three interconnected tables that must always stay in sync:









Table
Rows
Columns
Contains




Count / assay matrix
Genes/features
Samples
Raw counts, TPM, FPKM…


Sample metadata
Samples
Attributes
Condition, batch, sex…


Feature metadata
Genes/features
Attributes
Gene name, chromosome, GC%…



Keeping these three tables aligned by hand is error-prone.
SummarizedExperiment binds them into one object and guarantees they never go out of sync.

title: NGS Data Structures in R
text:
The SummarizedExperiment family
SummarizedExperiment (SE)
└── RangedSummarizedExperiment (RSE)   ← what you saw in class
    ├── DESeqDataSet         (DESeq2)
    ├── SingleCellExperiment (scRNA-seq)
    └── …and many more
RangedSummarizedExperiment adds genomic coordinates (a GRanges object) to each row/feature, enabling range-based operations.

title: NGS Data Structures in R
text:
Package installation
# Install from Bioconductor
if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

BiocManager::install("SummarizedExperiment")

# Also very useful
BiocManager::install(c("GenomicRanges", "DESeq2", "tximeta"))

title: NGS Data Structures in R
text:
How to use these notes
Each chapter builds on the previous one:

Structure — visual anatomy of an RSE object
Access & Manipulation — how to get data in and out
Workflow — from raw counts to a ready-to-analyse RSE







TipTip — Run the code!



Every code block is self-contained and can be run in a fresh R session after installing SummarizedExperiment.

title: 1  Structure of a RangedSummarizedExperiment
text:
1.1 The big picture
A RangedSummarizedExperiment (RSE) is best imagined as a rectangular container where rows are genomic features (genes, transcripts, peaks…) and columns are samples. Every slot is row-indexed or column-indexed, so subsetting one slot automatically subsets all others.
The RSE design solves a fundamental bookkeeping problem: in any NGS experiment you are juggling at least three interconnected tables — a count matrix, sample annotations, and feature annotations — that must always stay in sync. If even a single row gets swapped or a sample column is silently reordered, every downstream statistical result becomes wrong. RSE solves this by binding everything into one object where all subsetting operations propagate automatically.
Think of an RSE as a labelled data cube:

title: 1  Structure of a RangedSummarizedExperiment
text:
The assay matrix (blue) is the core table: rows = genes, columns = samples, cells = measurements (raw counts, TPM, log-CPM, …). Multiple assay layers can be stored simultaneously.
The rowRanges (green, left) are attached to the row axis — one genomic interval per gene, storing chromosome, start, end, and strand.
The rowData (pink, right) holds additional per-gene annotation columns (symbol, biotype, GC%) as a DataFrame.
The colData (yellow, bottom) holds per-sample metadata (condition, batch, sex, QC metrics) as a DataFrame.
The metadata (purple, bottom-right) is a free-form named list for experiment-level information that does not belong to any row or column.

Figure 1.1 — Anatomy of a RangedSummarizedExperiment. The assay matrix is the centre; all other slots are indexed to its rows or columns.






NoteHow to read this diagram



Each coloured block is one slot of the RSE object, accessed by its own function:








Colour
Slot
Key point




Blue
assay(s)
The measurement matrix. An RSE can hold multiple assays (e.g. counts and normcounts) as a named list, all sharing the same row/column dimensions.


Green
rowRanges
One GRanges interval per feature. Enables range operations: “which genes overlap this QTL?”


Pink
rowData
Annotation DataFrame for features: gene symbol, biotype, GC%, etc. (These are the mcols of the GRanges.)


Yellow
colData
Annotation DataFrame for samples: condition, batch, library size, QC metrics. This is what you pass to DESeq2 as your design.


Purple
metadata
A plain R list for anything else: organism, genome assembly, pipeline version, analysis date.



The arrows show indexing: subsetting rse[1:100, rse$condition == "treated"] simultaneously trims the blue matrix, the green ranges, the pink rowData, and the yellow colData. The purple metadata is never subsetted — it stays attached to every derived object.

Experiment-level free text, parameters…










NoterowData vs rowRanges — what’s the difference?



In a RangedSummarizedExperiment, rowRanges() always returns a GRanges object containing the genomic coordinates.
rowData() returns the mcols() (metadata columns) of that same GRanges — i.e., the non-coordinate per-feature annotations.
In a plain SummarizedExperiment (no ranges), rowRanges() returns NULL and rowData() returns the full per-feature DataFrame.

title: 1  Structure of a RangedSummarizedExperiment
text:
1.4 Dimensions and names
An RSE always has two dimensions accessible via dim():
dim(rse)
# [1] 20000   8      # 20 000 genes × 8 samples

nrow(rse)   # number of features
ncol(rse)   # number of samples

rownames(rse)  # feature identifiers (e.g. Ensembl IDs)
colnames(rse)  # sample names






ImportantThe golden rule of RSE — subsetting is synchronised



rse_sub <- rse[1:100, rse$condition == "treated"]
This simultaneously subsets:

the assay matrix(es) to rows 1–100 and treated columns
rowRanges to features 1–100
colData to treated samples only
rowData accordingly

You can never accidentally misalign rows and columns.

title: 1  Structure of a RangedSummarizedExperiment
text:
1.5 What does show() print?
When you type an RSE object name in the console, R calls show() and you see something like:
class: RangedSummarizedExperiment 
dim: 20000 8 
metadata(1): ''
assays(2): counts normcounts
rownames(20000): ENSG00000000003 ENSG00000000005 ...
rowData names(3): gene_id symbol biotype
colnames(8): S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 S6 S7 S8
colData names(4): Sample condition batch sex
Each line directly corresponds to one slot in the diagram above.

title: 2  Accessing & Manipulating an RSE
text:
2.1 Creating an RSE from scratch
This chapter covers the practical mechanics of working with an RSE: how to get data in and out of every slot, how to filter rows and columns, and how to combine multiple objects.
The key principle is that every accessor works as both a getter and a setter. Calling colData(rse) returns the sample metadata; calling colData(rse) <- new_df replaces it (with automatic dimension checking to prevent misalignment). The same pattern applies to every slot.
Although in practice you will load an RSE produced by a pipeline (see Chapter 3), it is instructive to build one manually.

title: 2  Accessing & Manipulating an RSE
text:
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(GenomicRanges)

## ── 1. Assay matrices ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
counts <- matrix(
  rpois(200, lambda = 500),   # 20 genes × 10 samples
  nrow = 20, ncol = 10,
  dimnames = list(
    paste0("ENSG", 1:20),     # row names = gene IDs
    paste0("S", 1:10)         # col names = sample IDs
  )
)

normcounts <- log2(counts + 1)  # a second assay layer

## ── 2. rowRanges (GRanges) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
gr <- GRanges(
  seqnames = c(rep("chr1", 10), rep("chr2", 10)),
  ranges   = IRanges(start = seq(1e4, 2e5, length.out = 20),
                     width = 1000),
  strand   = rep(c("+", "-"), 10),
  gene_id  = paste0("ENSG", 1:20),   # mcols
  symbol   = paste0("GENE", 1:20)    # mcols
)
names(gr) <- paste0("ENSG", 1:20)   # must match rownames(counts)

## ── 3. colData ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
col_df <- DataFrame(
  sample    = paste0("S", 1:10),
  condition = rep(c("treated", "control"), each = 5),
  batch     = rep(c("B1", "B2"), 5),
  sex       = sample(c("M", "F"), 10, replace = TRUE)
)
rownames(col_df) <- paste0("S", 1:10)   # must match colnames(counts)

## ── 4. Assemble ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rse <- SummarizedExperiment(
  assays    = list(counts = counts, normcounts = normcounts),
  rowRanges = gr,
  colData   = col_df,
  metadata  = list(organism = "Homo sapiens", pipeline = "tutorial")
)

rse   # inspect






TipKey: matching names



rownames(counts) must equal names(gr);
colnames(counts) must equal rownames(col_df).
If they don’t match, the constructor throws an error.

title: 2  Accessing & Manipulating an RSE
text:
2.2 Reading slots
Each slot has a dedicated accessor function. The plural form (e.g. assays()) returns the full container (a SimpleList or DataFrame), while the singular form (e.g. assay()) returns a single layer by name or index.

2.2.1 Assays
# All assay names
assayNames(rse)
# [1] "counts"     "normcounts"

# Get the raw count matrix (returns a plain matrix)
counts_mat <- assay(rse, "counts")
counts_mat <- assay(rse, 1)         # same — by position

# Get all assays as a SimpleList
all_assays <- assays(rse)

# Add a new assay
assay(rse, "logCPM") <- edgeR::cpm(counts_mat, log = TRUE)


2.2.2 rowRanges / rowData
# Full GRanges
rowRanges(rse)            # returns GRanges

# Metadata columns of the GRanges (= rowData)
rowData(rse)              # returns DataFrame
rowData(rse)$symbol       # single column as a vector

# Access via GRanges methods
seqnames(rowRanges(rse))  # chromosome of every feature
start(rowRanges(rse))     # start positions
width(rowRanges(rse))     # feature widths in bp
strand(rowRanges(rse))    # strand


2.2.3 colData
The colData slot is the most-used slot in practice — it holds condition, batch, and all other sample-level variables you will reference in your statistical design.
colData(rse)              # full DataFrame
colData(rse)$condition    # one column

# Shorthand with $ (very convenient!)
rse$condition             # identical to colData(rse)$condition
rse$batch

# Add a new sample annotation
rse$RIN <- c(9.1, 8.7, 9.3, 8.9, 9.0,
             8.5, 9.2, 8.8, 9.1, 8.6)  # RNA integrity






TipThe $ shorthand



rse$condition is shorthand for colData(rse)$condition. It works for reading and writing (rse$RIN <- ...). In practice, almost all filtering is written as rse[, rse$condition == "treated"] because it is far more readable than the long-form equivalent.




2.2.4 metadata
metadata(rse)             # returns a named list
metadata(rse)$organism    # one element
metadata(rse)$QC <- list(minRIN = 8, minDepth = 1e6)

title: 2  Accessing & Manipulating an RSE
text:
2.3 Subsetting
Subsetting uses standard [row, col] syntax — just like a matrix. The critical difference from plain matrix subsetting is that all slots are subsetted together: the assay matrices, rowRanges, rowData, and colData all shrink in lock-step. You cannot accidentally produce a mismatched object.
You can subset by integer index, character name, or a logical vector — whichever is most convenient:
## By index
rse[1:5, 1:3]

## By name
rse["ENSG3", "S2"]

## By logical vector — keep treated samples only
rse[, rse$condition == "treated"]

## Keep only chr1 features
rse[seqnames(rowRanges(rse)) == "chr1", ]

## Combine both
rse_sub <- rse[
  seqnames(rowRanges(rse)) == "chr1",
  rse$condition == "treated"
]
dim(rse_sub)


  

  
  Before [rows, cols]

  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  subset
  m × n
  
  cols 1-3
  rows 1-3

  
  →
  rse[1:3, 1:3]

  
  After (all slots synced)

  
  
  assay
  3 × 3

  
  
  rowRanges
  3 ranges

  
  
  colData
  3 samples

  
  
  metadata
  unchanged

  
  All slots automatically
  subsetted in sync ✓

Figure 2.1 — Subsetting an RSE synchronises every slot simultaneously.

title: 2  Accessing & Manipulating an RSE
text:
2.4 Merging RSEs — cbind and rbind
# Combine samples (same features, different samples)
rse_combined <- cbind(rse_batch1, rse_batch2)

# Combine features (same samples, different genomic regions)
rse_all <- rbind(rse_chr1, rse_chr2)






Warning



For cbind, both objects must have identical rowRanges (same features).
For rbind, both objects must have identical colData (same samples).

title: 2  Accessing & Manipulating an RSE
text:
2.5 Useful utility functions
# How many assays?
length(assays(rse))

# Feature names and dimensions
rownames(rse); colnames(rse); dim(rse)

# Quick summary of colData
summary(as.data.frame(colData(rse)))

# Which chromosomes are represented?
table(seqnames(rowRanges(rse)))

# Find features overlapping a region of interest
library(GenomicRanges)
query  <- GRanges("chr1", IRanges(1e4, 5e4))
hits   <- findOverlaps(rowRanges(rse), query)
rse_roi <- rse[queryHits(hits), ]

title: 3  NGS Workflow & File Structure
text:
3.1 Where does an RSE come from in practice?
In a real RNA-seq experiment you never build an RSE by hand. Instead, a quantification tool produces count files that are then loaded into R using a dedicated importer.
Two main loading strategies exist, depending on which quantifier you used:
tximeta is the gold-standard when possible: it downloads and attaches the matching transcript/gene annotation automatically, handles multi-mapping bias correctly with transcript-level uncertainty propagation, and produces a fully annotated RSE in one function call. Use the manual route when you started with a BAM-based alignment workflow or received a plain count matrix from a collaborator.

Figure 3.1 — Typical RNA-seq workflow. The RSE is the central hand-off object between upstream quantification and downstream statistical analysis.






NoteWhich loading path should I use?



Use tximeta (left path) whenever you ran Salmon or kallisto:

Automatically downloads the correct Ensembl / GENCODE annotation and populates rowRanges
Preserves transcript-level uncertainty for more statistically rigorous DE analysis
Works directly with DESeq2, edgeR, and fishpond without extra steps
One function call: rse <- tximeta(coldata) followed by rse_gene <- summarizeToGene(rse)

Use the manual approach (right path) when:

You used STAR + featureCounts or HISAT2 + HTSeq (BAM-based alignment)
You received a plain count matrix (e.g. from a collaborator) without quant.sf files
You need a custom GRanges object for rowRanges (e.g. from a non-standard annotation)

In both cases the end result is the same RSE object and all downstream tools work identically.

title: 3  NGS Workflow & File Structure
text:
3.2 Typical project file structure
A well-organised NGS project following Bioconductor conventions looks like this:
my_rnaseq_project/
│
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   ├── sample1_R1.fastq.gz
│   │   ├── sample1_R2.fastq.gz
│   │   └── ...
│   │
│   ├── counts/                        ← featureCounts / HTSeq output
│   │   ├── featureCounts_output.txt
│   │   └── featureCounts_output.txt.summary
│   │
│   ├── salmon/                        ← Salmon quantification output
│   │   ├── sample1/
│   │   │   ├── quant.sf               ← transcript-level counts
│   │   │   └── aux_info/
│   │   └── sample2/
│   │       └── quant.sf
│   │
│   ├── metadata/
│   │   └── sample_sheet.csv           ← colData source
│   │
│   └── rse/
│       └── rse_all_samples.rds        ← saved RSE object
│
├── analysis/
│   ├── 01_build_rse.R                 ← create & save RSE
│   ├── 02_qc.R                        ← quality control
│   ├── 03_DE.R                        ← differential expression
│   └── 04_visualisation.R
│
├── results/
│   ├── DE_tables/
│   └── plots/
│
└── my_rnaseq_project.Rproj

title: 3  NGS Workflow & File Structure
text:
3.3 Loading RSEs from common sources

3.3.1 From Salmon output via tximeta (recommended for RNA-seq)
tximeta is the gold-standard loader: it automatically attaches transcript/gene annotations and populates rowRanges.
library(tximeta)

# Build a sample sheet (one row per sample)
coldata <- data.frame(
  names  = c("S1", "S2", "S3", "S4"),
  files  = file.path("data/salmon",
                     c("S1","S2","S3","S4"),
                     "quant.sf"),
  condition = c("treated","treated","control","control"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Import — automatically downloads annotation & creates RSE
rse <- tximeta(coldata)

# Summarise to gene level (from transcript level)
rse_gene <- summarizeToGene(rse)


3.3.2 From featureCounts / HTSeq via base R
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(GenomicRanges)

# 1. Read the count matrix
fc <- read.table("data/counts/featureCounts_output.txt",
                 header = TRUE, skip = 1, row.names = 1)

# 2. Separate annotation columns from count columns
annot_cols  <- 1:5   # Chr, Start, End, Strand, Length
count_cols  <- 6:ncol(fc)

counts <- as.matrix(fc[, count_cols])
colnames(counts) <- gsub(".*Aligned\\.sortedByCoord.*", "",
                         colnames(counts))   # clean names

# 3. Build GRanges from the annotation columns
gr <- GRanges(
  seqnames = fc$Chr,
  ranges   = IRanges(fc$Start, fc$End),
  strand   = fc$Strand,
  gene_id  = rownames(fc),
  length   = fc$Length
)
names(gr) <- rownames(fc)

# 4. Read sample sheet → colData
col_df <- read.csv("data/metadata/sample_sheet.csv",
                   row.names = 1)

# 5. Assemble RSE
rse <- SummarizedExperiment(
  assays    = list(counts = counts),
  rowRanges = gr,
  colData   = col_df
)

# 6. Save for reuse
saveRDS(rse, "data/rse/rse_all_samples.rds")


3.3.3 Loading a saved RSE
rse <- readRDS("data/rse/rse_all_samples.rds")

title: 3  NGS Workflow & File Structure
text:
3.4 Handing off to DESeq2
Once you have an RSE with a counts assay, passing it to DESeq2 is one line:
library(DESeq2)

dds <- DESeqDataSet(rse, design = ~ batch + condition)

# DESeqDataSet is itself a subclass of RSE,
# so all RSE accessor functions still work:
dim(dds)
colData(dds)
rowRanges(dds)


  

  
  RSE
  counts + rowRanges + colData
  class: RangedSummarizedExperiment

  
  
  DESeqDataSet(rse,
  design = ~ condition)

  
  DESeqDataSet
  extends RSE
  + dispersion estimates
  class: DESeqDataSet

  
    
      
    
  

Figure 3.2 — A DESeqDataSet is a subclass of RSE; the transition is seamless.

title: 3  NGS Workflow & File Structure
text:
3.5 Quick cheat-sheet
## ── Inspect ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rse                          # print summary
dim(rse)                     # [features, samples]
dimnames(rse)                # list of rownames & colnames

## ── Assays ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
assayNames(rse)              # names of stored matrices
assay(rse)                   # first assay (usually "counts")
assay(rse, "normcounts")     # specific assay by name

## ── Features (rows) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rowRanges(rse)               # GRanges with coordinates
rowData(rse)                 # DataFrame with feature annotations
rownames(rse)                # character vector of IDs
nrow(rse)

## ── Samples (columns) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
colData(rse)                 # DataFrame with sample metadata
rse$condition                # shorthand column access
colnames(rse)
ncol(rse)

## ── Experiment metadata ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
metadata(rse)

## ── Subsetting ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rse[genes, samples]          # indices, names, or logical
rse[, rse$condition == "treated"]
rse["ENSG00000000003", ]

## ── Combine ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cbind(rse1, rse2)            # add samples (same features)
rbind(rse1, rse2)            # add features (same samples)

## ── Save / load ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
saveRDS(rse, "rse.rds")
rse <- readRDS("rse.rds")
